questions.stem: In how many different queues can 5 boys and 3 girls stand if the 3 girls must stand next to one another?
questions.hint: Treat the three girls as one block first, then arrange the girls within that block.

keyPoints.text: the 3 girls must stand next to one another
keyPoints.note: Group the girls as one block before counting the arrangements.

steps.explain: Treat the three girls as one block. The five boys and this block make six objects to arrange.
The three girls can change order within their block in 3! ways.
Multiply the independent choices to count every valid queue exactly once.

questions.stem: Each of the letters A, A, C, H, M, and S is written on a separate card. The cards are drawn at random and placed next to each other to form a word. What is the probability that the word ASCHAM appears?
questions.hint: Count the distinct six-letter arrangements, remembering that the two A cards are identical in the word, then compare the single target arrangement with that total.

keyPoints.text: probability that the word ASCHAM appears
keyPoints.note: There is exactly one favourable arrangement: ASCHAM.
Because the two A cards show the same letter, divide the factorial count by 2!.

steps.explain: There are six cards, but swapping the two A cards does not create a different visible word.
Evaluate the number of distinct arrangements.
Only one of these arrangements spells ASCHAM, so probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

questions.stem: Five boys and five girls are seated at a round table. How many arrangements have Robert and Hannah sitting together?
questions.hint: Treat Robert and Hannah as one block. Then arrange that block and the other eight people around the circle, and count the two orders inside the block.

keyPoints.note: Make the pair one object before arranging the people.
Circular arrangements of 9 distinct objects have (9−1)! orders.

steps.explain: Combine Robert and Hannah into one block. This gives 9 objects around the table.
Circular arrangements of 9 objects are counted up to rotation.
Robert and Hannah can swap places inside their block in 2 ways.

questions.stem: Nine points are given, with exactly four lying on one straight line and no other three collinear. How many triangles can be formed using the points as vertices?
questions.hint: Count all triples of points, then remove triples chosen entirely from the four collinear points.

keyPoints.note: A triple from those four points does not make a triangle.

keyPoints.text: four lying on one straight line
keyPoints.note: Only the all-collinear triples need to be removed.

steps.explain: Remove the triples selected from the four collinear points; these do not form triangles.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of the fourth term in the expansion of \((3x-4)^6\)?
questions.hint: The fourth term uses the binomial index r = 3. Substitute r = 3 into the general term.

keyPoints.note: Terms are counted from r = 0, so the fourth term has r = 3.

steps.explain: Write the general term and select r = 3 for the fourth term.
Separate the numerical coefficient from x³.
Multiply the factors, keeping the negative sign from the odd power of −4.
